original_question: Let f(x_1,...,x_n) be a complex polynomial such that all moments M_m = integral_[0,1]^n f(x_1,...,x_n)^m dx_1...dx_n vanish for every m >= 1. Must f be identically zero?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 (Vanishing Conjecture) in Section 1.1, with Proposition 1.2 providing the equivalent hypothesis and Theorem 1.3 explaining why the quantities Δ^m(P^{m+1}) are the relevant ones.
correct_elements: The draft at least has the right ambient flavor of asking about a complex polynomial and imposing a vanishing condition for every positive integer m. It also correctly uses a universal quantifier over all m >= 1.
missing_details: The paper is not about integral moments over [0,1]^n; the vanishing condition is differential-algebraic, involving iterates of the Laplace operator Δ applied to powers of the polynomial.
The ambient algebra is C[z_1,...,z_n] (or C[[z_1,...,z_n]] in Proposition 1.2), with z = (z_1,...,z_n).
The operator must be defined explicitly: Δ = Σ_{i=1}^n ∂^2/∂z_i^2.
The paper's main conjecture is restricted to homogeneous polynomials of degree 4.
The crucial hypothesis is Hessian nilpotency: Hes P = (∂^2 P/∂z_i∂z_j) is nilpotent.
Equivalently, by Proposition 1.2, for polynomials of order at least 2 one may assume Δ^m(P^m) = 0 for every m >= 1; this is the correct replacement for the draft's integral-moment hypothesis.
The conclusion in the paper is not that P must vanish identically.
The actual conclusion asks whether Δ^m(P^{m+1}) = 0 for all sufficiently large m.
The phrase "for all sufficiently large m" must be made precise as: there exists M such that for every integer m >= M, Δ^m(P^{m+1}) = 0.
If one uses the equivalent formulation from Proposition 1.2, one should note the order condition o(P) >= 2; for a homogeneous quartic polynomial this is automatic.
The nearby context from Theorem 1.3 is that these expressions Δ^m(P^{m+1}) occur as the coefficients in the deformed inversion pair Q_t, which explains why this exact sequence is studied.
refined_question: Let n >= 1, let P(z_1,...,z_n) be a homogeneous polynomial of degree 4 in C[z_1,...,z_n], and let Δ = Σ_{i=1}^n ∂^2/∂z_i^2. Assume that P is Hessian nilpotent, i.e. its Hessian matrix Hes P = (∂^2 P/∂z_i∂z_j) is nilpotent. Must it follow that there exists an integer M such that Δ^m(P(z)^{m+1}) = 0 for every m >= M?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, using Proposition 1.2, one may ask: if P(z) in C[z_1,...,z_n] is homogeneous of degree 4 and satisfies Δ^m(P(z)^m) = 0 for every m >= 1, must there exist M such that Δ^m(P(z)^{m+1}) = 0 for every m >= M?
justification: The paper's exact opening target is the Vanishing Conjecture, not an integral-moment problem and not a uniqueness statement P ≡ 0. Section 1.1 formulates the conjecture for homogeneous degree-4 Hessian nilpotent polynomials. Proposition 1.2 then shows that Hessian nilpotency is equivalent to the condition Δ^m(P^m)=0 for all m >= 1, so this is the only paper-approved alternate formulation of the hypothesis. Theorem 1.3 supplies the immediate nearby context by expressing the deformed inversion pair Q_t in terms of the sequence Δ^m(P^{m+1}), which is why the conjecture asks for eventual vanishing of exactly these terms.
